title: How Far Is Far? Measuring Space

pages.text: The lights go out across the neighbourhood, and suddenly the sky is full of stars. How far away are they? Accra to Tamale is about 600 kilometres by road. A kilometre is a good unit for that journey. It is a poor unit for space. The Sun is about 150 million kilometres from Earth. Imagine a trotro that could drive there at a steady 100 kilometres an hour, with no stops for passengers. The trip would take about 171 years. And the Sun is our nearest star. For everything farther away, the numbers in kilometres become too long to read. Astronomers needed bigger units. They use two: the astronomical unit and the light-year.

pages.text: An astronomical unit, or AU, is the average distance between Earth and the Sun: about 150 million kilometres. So Earth is 1 AU from the Sun. This makes distances inside the Solar System easy to compare. Mercury, the closest planet, is about 0.4 AU from the Sun. Mars is about 1.5 AU. Jupiter is about 5 AU. Neptune, the farthest planet, is about 30 AU. You can see at once that Neptune is thirty times as far from the Sun as we are. Try saying that in kilometres: 4,500,000,000.

pages.text: Nothing travels faster than light. The speed of light in empty space is about 300,000 kilometres every second. That is fast enough to circle Earth more than seven times in one second. Even so, space is so large that light needs time to cross it. Sunlight takes about 8 minutes and 20 seconds to reach us. When you watch the Sun set over the sea at Cape Coast, you are seeing light that left the Sun more than eight minutes earlier. Light from Neptune takes about four hours to arrive.

pages.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. It is a unit of distance, not of time. One light-year is about 9.5 trillion kilometres (9.5 million million), or about 63,000 AU. Astronomers use light-years for the distances between stars. The nearest star to the Sun is a small red star called Proxima Centauri. It is about 4.2 light-years away. Its two bright neighbours, Alpha Centauri A and B, are about 4.4 light-years away. The light you see from them tonight began its journey more than four years ago. Looking far into space always means looking back in time.

pages.alt: The night sky with the Sun as a small yellow dot linked by a dotted line to a small red star labelled Proxima Centauri, 4.2 light-years, beside a bright pair labelled Alpha Centauri A and B.

pages.text: With these units we can write our full address. We live on Earth, a planet in the Solar System. The Sun is one of at least 100 billion stars in a galaxy called the Milky Way, which is about 100,000 light-years across. The Milky Way belongs to a small cluster of galaxies called the Local Group. And the Local Group is one tiny part of the observable universe, which holds hundreds of billions of galaxies. Some estimates go as high as two trillion. Earth, Solar System, Milky Way, Local Group, universe: that is where we are.

pages.text: To feel these distances, shrink them. Let 1 metre stand for 1 AU. Put the Sun on the goal line of a football pitch. Earth is one step away. Jupiter is about 5 metres out. Neptune is 30 metres out, still short of the halfway line. Voyager 1, the most distant spacecraft ever launched, would be about 173 metres away, well beyond the far goal. And the nearest star? On this scale it is about 270 kilometres away. If your Sun is in Accra, the next star is beyond Kumasi. Between them lies almost nothing at all.

activities.question: Jupiter is about 5 AU from the Sun. What does that tell you?
options: Jupiter is 5 million kilometres from the Sun
Jupiter is about five times as far from the Sun as Earth is
Light takes five years to reach Jupiter

activities.question: What does a light-year measure?
options: The time sunlight takes to reach Earth
The distance light travels in one year

activities.question: A star is 10 light-years away. When did the light you see tonight leave it?
